title: The Fall of Lady Babylon
summary: Babylon, pictured as a pampered royal lady, is told to come down from her throne, sit in the dust, and grind grain like a slave. God explains that he handed his people over to her in his anger, but she showed them no mercy and imagined she would be queen forever, saying of herself what only God can say. Widowhood and the loss of children will come on her in a single day, and her famous sorcerers and astrologers will be unable to save her or even themselves.
story: Chapter 46 showed Babylon's gods bowed down and carried away. Chapter 47 turns to the city itself. The empire that destroyed Jerusalem and deported its people seemed permanent to the exiles, and this chapter is the prophet's answer to that impression. Babylon is not the queen of the world; she is a creature who forgot that she held power only because God allowed it. After this chapter the focus shifts back to Israel (chapter 48), whose release depends on Babylon's fall. The chapter also shapes the rest of the Bible's imagination: Babylon becomes a name for every proud power that sets itself in God's place.
historical:
Babylon under the Chaldean dynasty was the greatest city of its day. Nebuchadnezzar II (who ruled about 605 to 562 BC) rebuilt it on a vast scale, with massive walls, the Ishtar Gate, the processional way, and the temple of Marduk. The empire controlled Mesopotamia, Syria, and Judah, and it was Nebuchadnezzar who took Jerusalem in 597 BC and destroyed it in 587 or 586 BC. Verse 6 recalls that cruelty, noting that even the elderly were given a heavy yoke.

The fall came in 539 BC, when Cyrus's forces took the city with little resistance. Babylon was not destroyed then; it remained a major city under the Persians. But its independence and its empire ended at once, and it never again ruled the world. Greater physical ruin came gradually over the following centuries, and by the Roman period much of the city was abandoned.
cultural:
The chapter's images come from the reversal of social status. Royal women lived in seclusion and luxury, veiled and carried; slave women ground grain by hand between millstones, the lowliest household labor (compare Exodus 11:5). To remove the veil and lift the skirt to wade through streams was to be treated as a captive, driven on foot across rivers into exile, exposed and shamed. The picture reverses what Babylon had done to Judah's daughters. Widowhood and the loss of children were the two great fears of an ancient woman, since both left her without protection or a future, and the city is threatened with both at once.

Babylon was famous in the ancient world for its learned diviners. Scholars there compiled vast collections of omens drawn from the heavens, from the livers of sacrificed sheep, and from strange events, and court astrologers watched the sky and reported to the king, especially at the new moon, when the month's signs were read. Incantations and spells were used to ward off disaster. Isaiah addresses this whole system as the city's supposed defense, and declares it useless.
literary: The chapter is a taunt song, a poem mocking a fallen enemy, similar in type to the song over the king of Babylon in chapter 14. It is spoken to Babylon in the second person throughout, with the exception of verse 4, where Israel breaks in with a brief confession of praise. The poem falls into stanzas, each opening with a command or accusation: go down and sit (verse 1), sit in silence (verse 5), hear this (verse 8), take your stand (verse 12). Babylon's own words are quoted three times, and twice she says “I am, and there is none besides me,” language that echoes God's own claim in chapter 45. The irony is pointed: the city talks like God and falls like stubble.

outline.t: The Virgin Daughter of Babylon brought down to the dust
No longer queen: judgment for showing no mercy
The secure one who said, 'I am, and there is none besides me'
Sorcerers and astrologers who cannot save

doctrines.note: Babylon is judged for pride (“I will be queen forever”), for cruelty (“You showed them no mercy”), and for claiming a place that belongs to God alone. Empires are accountable to God even when he uses them.
God says he placed his people under Babylon's control in his anger. Babylon's power was real but borrowed. When it forgot this, it lost everything “in a single day.”
Babylon's final idol is itself. Its claim “I am, and there is none besides me” is self-worship, and its reliance on spells and astrology is the attempt to control the future without God.

words.note: Gevereth, lady or mistress, the feminine of a word for master. Babylon is called the lady (queen) of kingdoms and says she will be lady forever. The title is used for a queen mother or the mistress of a household, and it captures Babylon's sense of permanent superiority.

Kesheph, sorcery, the use of magical arts to control events. The law of Moses forbade such practices in Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). Babylon's many sorceries are named as the defense it trusted, and the chapter shows them failing.

Rachamim, compassion or mercy, related to the word for womb. “You showed them no mercy.” God's anger had placed Judah in Babylon's hand, but Babylon went beyond judgment into cruelty, and for that it is judged.

Almanah, widow. In the ancient world a widow was one of the most vulnerable members of society, and the law often names her alongside the orphan and the foreigner. Babylon, who boasted she would never be a widow, will lose both husband and children in one day.

christ: The chapter's portrait of Babylon is taken up in the book of Revelation, which uses Babylon as a name for the great power opposed to God and his people. Revelation 18:7-8 closely echoes verses 7 to 9 here: the city says in her heart that she sits as queen, is no widow, and will never see mourning, and her plagues come in a single day. In Revelation, Babylon's fall clears the way for the marriage of the Lamb and the coming of the new Jerusalem. The connection to Christ is thus through the larger story: the proud power that claims to be god is brought down, and the one who humbled himself is exalted. Jesus's teaching that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11), states the principle this chapter dramatizes.

hard.q: If God handed his people to Babylon, why does he judge Babylon for what it did to them? And what of the chapter's harsh images?
hard.a:
The chapter itself answers the first question. God says he gave his people into Babylon's hand, but Babylon “showed them no mercy” and acted from pride, not from any sense of serving God's justice. Scripture regularly draws this line: a nation may be the instrument of judgment and still be accountable for its own motives and cruelty (compare Isaiah 10:5-15, where Assyria is judged for the same reason). God's use of a power does not make everything that power does right.

The second difficulty is the imagery of shame in verses 2 and 3, a humiliated woman exposed. The picture is drawn from the real treatment of captive women in ancient warfare, the treatment Babylon had inflicted on others, and it is turned on the city personified as a woman. Some readers find such imagery troubling in itself, and it should not be read as approving the abuse of women. Most interpreters understand it as a vivid reversal: the city that stripped and enslaved others will be stripped of its own glory. The target is the empire, not women.

questions: Babylon said, “I will be queen forever,” and did not consider the outcome. Where are people or institutions today tempted to think their power is permanent?
Babylon was judged not simply for being powerful but for showing no mercy. How should those with power treat those under them?
Babylon trusted astrologers and spells to secure its future. What are the modern ways people try to control the future without trusting God?
